/building/autonomous-ai-blog/.body:
Update, August 2026: the public feed this system publishes is now labeled as the machine-published Digest and is no longer the front door of the site. The system itself remains the exhibit. Publishing can be paused at any time with the PIPELINE_ENABLED repository variable.

The Goal

I wanted a blog that could publish daily analysis of AI news under my real name, without me writing every post and without the output reading like AI slop.

The hard part was never generating text. The hard part was everything around the text: finding the right stories, avoiding rumors, not repeating the same topic on day 30, citing real sources, and knowing when a draft was not good enough to publish.

The test I set was simple: could the site run for months, with no human approval loop, and still remain something I would put my name on?

What I Built

Version 1 was an n8n workflow: one curated YouTube transcript in, one blog post out. Gemini and GPT-5.5 handled the writing, and a 40-point QA rubric checked the finished draft.

It worked, but it exposed the real problem. The system could only see one source at a time, and it kept a history of covered topics that it never actually consulted. By week three, it was repeating itself.

Version 2 was a ground-up rebuild in TypeScript.

The new pipeline runs every day on GitHub Actions at 13:00 UTC. It ingests roughly 36 sources, including official lab blogs, arXiv, GitHub releases, Hacker News, Reddit, YouTube transcripts, and trade press for the niches I care about.

Every item is embedded, clustered into distinct stories, and checked against a vector memory of everything already published. Only genuinely new stories move forward.

The strongest stories become long-form pieces written by Claude Opus 4.8. The rest become shorter notes written by GPT-5.5. GPT-5.5 then grades every draft against an editorial rubric in a separate review pass, and only passing drafts publish. Failed pieces are saved as drafts instead of being deleted or shipped.

Each published post also receives generated artwork in one of five rotating art directions, structured data for search engines and AI assistants, and semantically related-post links computed from the same embeddings. A Telegram digest tells me what happened each day. Most days, that digest is the only part I read.

How It Works

The daily loop is:

ingest → embed → cluster → dedup against memory → rank → select → synthesize → gate → images → publish → digest

A few pieces do most of the work.

The dedup memory is Postgres with pgvector. Every published post lives there as an embedding, and a new story only survives if it is far enough from what came before.

Selection is not purely merit-based. A few beats I care about get one reserved slot per day, because a tier-two trade story will never outrank an arXiv paper on raw signal. A reserved slot is still not a guaranteed publish. The editorial gate can reject it.

Once a week, the pipeline attempts a deep dive: a 2,000-plus-word pillar piece that is only allowed to anchor on primary sources, links out to its most related existing posts, and has to clear a higher bar than daily notes. If the week’s material is too thin, it skips rather than shipping filler.

The entire system is controlled by one repo variable, so I can pause publishing with a settings change instead of a code revert.

Editorial Review

Every draft is graded in a separate pass by a reviewer that sees only the title and the draft. The reviewer is GPT-5.5. Flagship pieces and weekly deep dives are written by Claude Opus 4.8, so for those the reviewer is a different model from the writer. Daily notes are written by GPT-5.5, so for those the reviewer is the same model as the writer, running as a separate pass with its own instructions.

The reviewer scores four things from 1 to 10: originality, voice match, factual defensibility, and reader value. A daily note needs 27 out of 40 to publish, a flagship needs 30, and a weekly deep dive needs 31.

The score is only half of the decision. The reviewer also lists critical fails, and a single one sends the piece to drafts whatever it scored. Examples: hiding the primary source, a thin summary of one source dressed up as analysis, fabricated statistics or claims, a title the body contradicts, or price predictions and investment advice in posts about crypto and digital assets.

No person approves a post before it publishes. That is the experiment, and it is also its main limit.

Transparency

The Digest is labeled as machine-published everywhere it appears.

Every post opens with a note saying it was written and published by an autonomous system I built, that I am the publisher, and that I am accountable for it. The byline reads “KenAshe Digest (automated) · Ken Ashe, publisher.” The structured data says the same thing: the automated system is the author, and I am the publisher.

Posts name the sources they are based on, and since July 2026 those sources are also recorded with each post and published in its structured data. The disclosure page explains what is written by me, what is written by the system, and how corrections work.

Results So Far

As of November 25, 2026, the repository holds 1,610 Digest posts dated from May 14, 2026. Of those, 1,399 are published and 211 were held back as drafts.

I also measure whether any of this gets found. Once a month, 12 fixed, unbranded search queries are run against a retrieval engine, and the run records whether kenashe.ai appears in the top 25 results. It appeared for 1 of 12 queries in August, 1 in September, 2 in October, and 1 in November 2026. The queries are frozen so the trend cannot be flattered by rewording them.

An AI-assisted news site has cited the Digest as a source. I wrote about what that does and does not prove in My automated blog got cited.

Update, November 25, 2026: search visibility fell sharply. Google Search Console recorded 4,460 impressions and 52 clicks for kenashe.ai from November 13 to 16. From November 20 to 23 it recorded 112 impressions and 3 clicks. That is about 97.5% fewer impressions and about 94.2% fewer clicks. The decline began on November 20, while Google’s November 2026 core update was rolling out.

What is confirmed. Several automated articles that had been indexed, and one original tutorial, were later found to be no longer indexed. A technical investigation found no obvious technical fault that explains the decline. The technical audit counted 2,086 of the 2,124 sitemap URLs, about 98%, as Digest posts or tag pages.

What is not confirmed. Google has not said why. My working hypothesis is that its systems reassessed the site as a whole, and that the volume of automated pages next to a small amount of original work was a factor. That is a hypothesis. I am not claiming that Google penalized the site for publishing AI-generated content, and I have no evidence that it did.

November 25, 2026: I initially excluded the Digest and its archives from search indexing. That was a response to the drop, not evidence that exclusion improves rankings.

November 26, 2026: discovery across platforms. Published Digest articles, the blog landing page and the topic hubs are eligible for indexing again. The tag directory helps readers browse the archive. Individual tag listings with fewer than three published articles offer little choice, so only those listings are excluded. I’ll track search traffic and AI citations separately; eligibility does not guarantee either. The historical archive is public. This indexing decision does not restart publishing.

Limitations

Most posts respond to a single source. Of the 1,143 published posts that record their sources, 1,043 cite exactly one. The gate rejects thin summaries, but a commentary on one paper or one announcement is still a commentary on one source.

The reviewer is a model. It catches a lot. It is not a person reading the piece, and I do not read posts before they publish.

Volume outweighs everything else on the site. About ten posts a day adds up to 1,399 machine-written posts next to nine essays I directed myself. That is why I chose to present the Digest as an experiment rather than a search-driven publication.

What Broke & What I Learned

Plenty broke. The recurring theme was that the model was almost never the problem. The plumbing was.

Feed text is hostile input. Titles from academic feeds carry LaTeX and characters that can break the formats they are written into. One post took the production site down at build time. Everything the pipeline ingests is now sanitized as untrusted input, and there are regression tests for the exact failures.

Silent failure is the dangerous kind. At one point the pipeline was committing posts successfully and the site simply never updated, because the hosting platform quietly skipped deploys from commit authors it did not recognize. Another time, a selection path skipped every week without explaining why. The fix both times was the same: log the inputs to every silent decision, and make the daily digest say what did not happen, not just what did.

Verify access, not existence. I once swapped in a newly released model whose ID was real and documented. My account did not have access yet. The next run published zero posts. Every risky change now goes through shadow mode, which runs the full pipeline and publishes nothing.

Quality is a selection problem before it is a writing problem. Early deep dives kept failing the editorial gate for building confidently on rumors. No amount of prompt engineering fixed it, because the problem was upstream: the pipeline was choosing commentary-heavy stories to go deep on. Requiring a primary source before a pillar can even be attempted fixed in one change what three prompt revisions could not.

The gate has to be independent. The reviewer runs as a separate pass and reads only the draft. For flagship pieces it is also a different model than the writer. For daily notes it is the same model, which is a weaker check. When posts kept failing for vague sourcing, the durable fix was to tell the writer the standard it would be judged against. The pass rate nearly doubled, and every post now names its primary source.

Outcome

The Autonomous AI Blog launched in June 2026.

Scheduled publishing is paused. The historical archive remains publicly accessible, and the underlying application and publishing pipeline are preserved.

During its daily run, the system typically published roughly ten posts, each sourced, illustrated, deduplicated and reviewed automatically. On most days, my involvement was limited to reviewing the Telegram digest. Pieces that did not pass were saved as drafts.

The system has survived model outages, feed rate limits, a GitHub Actions outage, and its own bugs while keeping the daily cadence intact.

The repository contains the architecture and decision log needed to support a future handoff to another engineer or agent.

/building/sir-pitches-a-lot/.title: Sir Pitches-a-Lot – Ken Ashe
/building/sir-pitches-a-lot/.summary: A HyperAgent competition agent that researched an anonymized founder target, pitched Lucky Domains, and generated a personalized landing page campaign designed around one question: would they reply?
/building/sir-pitches-a-lot/.description: A HyperAgent competition agent that researched an anonymized founder target, pitched Lucky Domains, and generated a personalized landing page campaign designed around one question: would they reply?
/building/sir-pitches-a-lot/.body:
The Goal

The challenge was to build an agent that could create a mini outreach campaign for a matched target, not just write a single cold email.

The product was Lucky Domains, my domain acquisition and SEO strategy business. The target was a specific founder at a specific company, but I kept the public version anonymized.

The win condition was simple: would they reply?

That changed the project. The real challenge was not writing one good pitch. It was designing an agent that could repeatedly produce a good campaign under competition constraints.

The campaign needed to feel specific, useful, credible, and founder-to-founder. It also needed to support more than email. Pages, videos, social media concepts, mini decks, visuals, teardowns, and useful artifacts were all valid ways to pitch the target.

What I Built

I built Sir Pitches-a-Lot, a reusable HyperAgent system prompt designed for an Airtable outreach competition.

The name was intentionally unserious. The agent’s behavior was not.

The final shipped artifact was a reusable agent prompt plus a target-specific Lucky Domains campaign package. For this run, HyperAgent generated a personalized landing page as the main creative asset.

Sir Pitches-a-Lot was designed to create a complete campaign package, including:

  • A research hook
  • A fit thesis
  • A first-touch email
  • A follow-up sequence
  • A personalized creative asset
  • A clear call to action
  • A shareable campaign package

The agent was built using the same structured prompt framework I have been using across agent experiments: identity, context, instructions, criteria, and examples.

How It Works

The agent workflow is:

brief → research → trigger selection → fit thesis → email sequence → asset choice → landing page → campaign package → QA

Sir Pitches-a-Lot starts with the Airtable Battle Brief, the matched target, and the product being pitched.

It researches the target and company, then looks for a fresh and relevant hook from the last 6 to 12 months. If it finds a real trigger, it uses that as the opening angle. If research is thin, it follows a fallback ladder: target-specific trigger, company-specific trigger, observable workflow or business model fact, and finally a clearly labeled assumption.

That fallback ladder mattered because AI-generated outreach has an obvious failure mode: fake personalization. The agent was explicitly told not to invent research, not to treat stale information as current, and not to present assumptions as facts.

Once it has a credible hook, the agent builds a narrow fit thesis around why Lucky Domains could matter to that target now. It then drafts a concise first-touch email, follow-ups that add new value, and a low-friction CTA that a founder could answer quickly.

The creative asset is chosen based on what would most increase reply probability. The default preference is a teardown, audit, opportunity map, workflow map, or landing page rather than a generic product deck. In this run, the strongest format was a personalized landing page.

What Broke & What I Learned

The first version of the prompt over-produced.

It created a complete campaign report, but the win condition was not “who can write the longest campaign.” The win condition was “would they reply?” That forced the prompt to become tighter and more practical.

The real product was the agent. The competition was not just about producing one polished pitch. It rewarded the ability to build an agent that could research, reason, choose an asset format, write the campaign, and package the result.

The asset choice mattered. A generic deck would not prove much. A personalized landing page gave the pitch a more concrete shape and made the outreach feel built for the target rather than copied from a template.

Personalization can become hallucination. Without hard constraints, an outreach agent will be tempted to create hooks that sound plausible but are not real. The fallback ladder became one of the most important parts of the prompt.

Submission format mattered. The brief asked for a campaign share link, not a pile of disconnected assets. The final agent was updated to build one shareable campaign package and embed the creative asset inside it when possible.

The best CTA is low-friction. A meeting request is expensive. A one-word reply to receive a teardown, mockup, map, or short walkthrough is much easier to answer.

Outcome

Sir Pitches-a-Lot shipped as a working HyperAgent competition agent.

It created a tailored Lucky Domains campaign for an anonymized founder target and generated a personalized landing page as the primary campaign asset.

The project clarified an important distinction for me: building with AI is not just about getting one strong output. The bigger opportunity is designing agents that can repeatedly produce useful work under real constraints.

This was a small project, but it pointed toward a larger idea I keep coming back to: the best AI systems are not just clever. They are structured, honest, useful, and built to ship.

/writing/4-tips-for-making-ai-videos-tha.title: 4 Tips for Making AI Videos That Feel Like Films – Ken Ashe
/writing/4-tips-for-making-ai-videos-tha.h1: 4 Tips for Making AI Videos That Feel Like Films
/writing/4-tips-for-making-ai-videos-tha.meta: By Ken Ashe · November 20, 2026 · 4:49 video · Human-directed, AI-assisted
/writing/4-tips-for-making-ai-videos-tha.description: A mug that broke in the wrong place, a reach that changed the story, and a piano performance that worked where sound effects didn’t. Four lessons from making Returning Your Things.
/writing/4-tips-for-making-ai-videos-tha.body:
I knew my actors needed character sheets. I didn’t expect my coffee mug to need one, too. In one picture, a blue flower was painted in the middle of the cup. In another, the same flower was attached to the broken handle. Both pictures looked fine until I put them next to each other.

These are the four things I’d do again. If you’d rather see the story before the spoilers, watch Returning Your Things first. The film is 1:54; the walkthrough below is 4:49.

1. Give recurring objects a reference sheet.

Watch from 0:12

I had a sheet for each actor so I could recognize the same two people on a spring rooftop, by the water in summer, and across a kitchen table. The objects needed references for a different reason: they’re how you know whose memory you’re in. A man picks up a piece of pottery in the snow. Cut to the kitchen. You need to recognize that cup without anybody saying a word.

I liked the broken piece. The fix was to go back to the intact mug and move the painted flower closer to the handle. That’s the detail I’d put on a prop sheet next time: not just what the object looks like, but which part of it the audience will see again.

2. Tell the AI what to keep, not just what to change.

Watch from 1:36

In shot 15, the wind takes her hat. I liked the man’s reach, but he was looking to the side instead of at the brim. The next image fixed his gaze and pitched his whole body forward. Now he looked determined to catch it. That was right for the summer memory and wrong for the winter street, where he’s about to let it go.

The most useful part of my next note was “the original picture was fine.” Once I named what to preserve, I could ask for the small change I actually wanted.

3. Lock the pictures before you work on sound.

Watch from 2:32

I made a silent review copy with each shot number and its start time underneath the picture. Instead of scrubbing around for “that bit in the snow,” I could say “shot 15” and keep the discussion about his eyes. I settled the pictures and their timing before trying the sound again.

That also made it easier to turn something down. I tried footsteps in the snow and a gust as the hat blew away. Even with the gust in the right place, I didn’t want it in the finished film. Getting a sound in sync and wanting to hear it are two different decisions.

4. Choose music for the story, not for every cut.

Watch from 3:44

The first piano score didn’t feel consistent to me. I asked whether there was a classical melody in the public domain that we could use instead. I ended up choosing Donald Betts playing Schumann’s Of Foreign Lands and Peoples. The composition and the performance have separate rights; Musopen released this particular recording into the public domain.

My test was the hat. In summer, he puts it back on her head. In the next picture he’s walking alone, with the hat behind him in the snow. The pianist keeps playing. I didn’t need a new cue to tell me how to feel about that cut.

/writing/bambu-lab-burr-puzzle-solution/.meta: By Ken Ashe · November 6, 2026 · 2:44 video · Human-directed, AI-assisted
/writing/bambu-lab-burr-puzzle-solution/.description: How to solve the Bambu Lab Burr Puzzle: a 2:44 overhead video showing how the six pieces go together, solved twice, with links that jump straight to each step.
/writing/bambu-lab-burr-puzzle-solution/.body:
I printed the Burr Puzzle on my Bambu Lab printer and figured putting it together would be easy. It wasn’t. Six pieces turned out to be a lot more complicated than I expected.

I looked for video tutorials, but the ones I found were hard to follow. So I made my own.

The goal was a simple, clear demonstration you can follow while you assemble the puzzle yourself. I filmed it from directly overhead and solved it twice: first with a teal set of pieces, then with a red set. If the first walkthrough doesn’t click, the second gives you another look at the same solution.

What you’ll learn

The video shows how each of the six pieces is oriented and how they interlock, from loose pieces on the table to a finished puzzle. Both sets start laid out side by side. I assemble the teal puzzle first, then repeat the whole solution with the red pieces.

Jump to the solution

  1. 0:00 Introduction and piece layout
  2. 0:33 First assembly walkthrough (teal puzzle)
  3. 1:44 Second assembly walkthrough (red puzzle)
  4. 2:30 Final assembly and completed puzzles

Each link starts the video above at that point. Open it in a new tab to watch on YouTube instead.

Helpful tips

  • Lay out your pieces the way I do at the start. Same order, same orientation. It makes it much easier to tell which piece I’m picking up.
  • Pause between steps. Get each piece into the same position as mine before you move on. Slowing the playback speed on YouTube helps too.
  • Watch it again in red. If a step doesn’t make sense the first time, jump to the second walkthrough at 1:44 and follow the red pieces.
  • Still stuck? Leave a comment on the video with the timestamp where you got lost, and I’ll do my best to help.

Watch it on YouTube

If this helped you solve your puzzle, the original video is on YouTube. I post hands-on builds and technology experiments on my channel, and you can see more of what I’ve been testing on Building and in my Writing.

This is my own walkthrough of a puzzle I printed. It isn’t an official Bambu Lab tutorial, and I’m not affiliated with Bambu Lab.

/writing/ashe-family-coat-of-arms/.title: The Ashe Family Coat of Arms: A Cockatrice and a Guinness Connection – Ken Ashe
/writing/ashe-family-coat-of-arms/.h1: The Ashe Family Coat of Arms: A Cockatrice and a Guinness Connection
/writing/ashe-family-coat-of-arms/.meta: By Ken Ashe · Originally published April 6, 2016 · Updated October 2026 · Human-written original, AI-assisted refresh
/writing/ashe-family-coat-of-arms/.description: A search for the Ashe family coat of arms led to a mythical cockatrice, a Latin motto, Shakespeare, and an unexpected Guinness connection.
/writing/ashe-family-coat-of-arms/.body:
Years ago, I started searching online for the Ashe family coat of arms. I expected to find a shield, maybe a motto, and that would be it. Instead, I found a mythical creature I’d never heard of, a reference in Shakespeare, and an unexpected connection to one of my favorite beers: Guinness.

The shield: two black chevronels

The basic design is simple: a silver (or white) shield with two narrow black chevrons. The formal heraldic description is “Argent, two chevronels sable.” In heraldry, argent means silver and sable means black.

It’s the design I kept seeing on coat-of-arms websites—the kind that will happily print your supposed family crest on a mug. But digging into the historical references turned out to be more interesting than buying the mug.

One important distinction I’ve learned since I first wrote this: coats of arms historically belonged to particular people and family lines, not everyone with the same surname. The version I found is listed for the Ashe family of Ashfield, County Meath, Ireland. I haven’t established a genealogical connection between that line and my own.

The motto: Non nobis sed omnibus

The Latin motto translates as “Not for us, but for all.”

Some historical descriptions also put a single word above the shield: “Fight.” Put the two together and you get a reading I like: “Fight, not for us, but for all.” That’s my interpretation of the two inscriptions, rather than a literal translation of one continuous motto.

The cockatrice

The creature at the top of the coat of arms is a cockatrice. I had no idea what that was when I started researching this.

A cockatrice is a mythical creature usually depicted with a rooster’s head and a dragonlike or serpentine body. According to some legends, it could kill with a look.

Apparently, this was a familiar enough creature in Britain that Shakespeare referenced it in Richard III:

A cockatrice hast thou hatch’d to the world,
Whose unavoided eye is murderous.

In heraldic language, this particular Ashe crest is described as a gold cockatrice with a red comb and wattles. The black-and-white drawing doesn’t show those colors, but it does a pretty good job of making the creature look intimidating.

The unexpected Guinness connection

Here’s where the research took an interesting turn.

I came across an old Guinness Extra Stout “Cockatrice Brand” label. There was that familiar creature again—but look closely at the bottom of the label. It says “Bottled by T. F. Ashe & Nephew, Liverpool.”

The label identifies T. F. Ashe & Nephew of Liverpool as the bottler. I haven’t established whether that company was connected to the family associated with this coat of arms, or to my own family. But seeing the Ashe name and that familiar cockatrice on a Guinness label was still a pretty great discovery.

Still an interesting piece of Ashe history

I originally published this research in 2016. Looking back at it now, I think the best part isn’t the claim of having a family coat of arms. It’s how one question led to another: a shield, a Latin motto, a mythical creature, Shakespeare, and finally a Guinness label.

Not a bad outcome for a little curiosity about a last name.

Watch the story (50 seconds)

Sources and further reading

  • Bernard Burke, The General Armory of England, Scotland, Ireland, and Wales (London, 1884), Supplement, “Ashe (Ashfield, co. Meath)”: arms, cockatrice crest, and the mottoes “Fight” above the shield and “Non nobis sed omnibus” below.
  • Fairbairn’s Book of Crests of the Families of Great Britain and Ireland, vol. 1 (1905 edition), p. 21, “Ashe of Ashfield, Ireland”: the cockatrice crest with both mottoes.
  • John Burke and John Bernard Burke, Encyclopædia of Heraldry, or General Armory of England, Scotland and Ireland (1851): the related Ashe of Sowton, Devonshire entry, with two chevrons and a cockatrice crest.
  • William Shakespeare, Richard III, Act 4, Scene 1, the Duchess of York’s lines.
  • Read the original April 2016 article on the Internet Archive.

/writing/iphone-18-pro-att-activation-fa.title: My iPhone 18 Pro Upgrade Failed. Then My Old Phone Lost Service Too. – Ken Ashe
/writing/iphone-18-pro-att-activation-fa.h1: My iPhone 18 Pro Upgrade Failed. Then My Old Phone Lost Service Too.
/writing/iphone-18-pro-att-activation-fa.meta: By Ken Ashe · October 10, 2026 · Firsthand account
/writing/iphone-18-pro-att-activation-fa.description: My AT&T iPhone 18 Pro upgrade failed and disabled cellular service on my old phone. Here's what happened, how activation eventually worked, and what I learned.
/writing/iphone-18-pro-att-activation-fa.body:
On Friday, October 9, I walked into an AT&T store with a working iPhone 16 Pro and a brand-new iPhone 18 Pro.

More than two and a half hours later, I walked out with two phones and no working cellular service on either one.

My new phone wouldn’t activate. Worse, during AT&T’s attempts to fix the problem, my original phone lost service too.

It was the beginning of a long holiday weekend. I have kids with their own schedules, and like most families, we rely on our phones to coordinate plans and stay in touch.

What concerned me most wasn’t that the new phone wouldn’t activate. Technology fails sometimes.

It was that the activation process left me without service on my existing phone, and AT&T’s own specialists couldn’t restore it.

And when the problem unexpectedly resolved the following day, I still had no idea what had changed.

It started with three new iPhones

On Wednesday, October 7, I ordered three new iPhones through AT&T for my family.

They arrived Thursday, and my wife attempted to upgrade from her iPhone 16 to an iPhone 18 Pro.

The activation failed.

Fortunately, her old phone continued working. We decided to visit an AT&T store the next day rather than continue troubleshooting ourselves.

On Friday, October 9, the AT&T store in Watchung, New Jersey, eventually activated her new phone using a new eSIM.

Then we tried mine.

My upgrade made things worse

I was upgrading from an iPhone 16 Pro to an iPhone 18 Pro.

The initial activation failed. The store representative attempted alternative methods, including issuing new eSIMs.

Those attempts also failed.

During the troubleshooting, my original iPhone 16 Pro lost its cellular connection.

Now neither phone worked.

I couldn’t simply abandon the upgrade and return to my old device. I had walked into the store with working cellular service, and now I had none.

I later captured a screenshot showing my original iPhone displaying SOS and a failed attempt to call 611, AT&T’s support number.

Even AT&T’s specialists couldn’t restore service

The store representative genuinely tried to help.

He spent approximately two hours on the phone with AT&T’s specialist support team. We worked with an initial specialist, escalated to a supervisor, and eventually contacted AT&T’s Wireless Account Lock department.

I spoke directly with that department as well.

The explanation I received was that repeated activation attempts had triggered a 48-hour account restriction that nobody could override.

I asked about restoring service to my original iPhone rather than continuing with the upgrade.

That couldn’t be accomplished either.

After more than two and a half hours in the store, I left without working cellular service on either device.

I had no written technical explanation of what had happened, why the restriction existed, or why my previously working phone couldn’t be restored.

The employee said he’d seen similar problems

During the troubleshooting, the AT&T representative mentioned something that caught my attention.

He told me these activation problems seemed to be common.

He described helping another customer on a recent evening, spending approximately two hours troubleshooting and staying after the store closed. According to him, they still couldn’t resolve that customer’s issue.

I can’t verify how widespread these failures are, but his experience made me curious enough to look for other reports.

I found a September 19 discussion on Reddit in which another customer described an unsuccessful iPhone 18 Pro activation, loss of cellular service on both the old and new phones, and an initial estimate of 48–72 hours before the problem might be resolved.

That customer later reported that service returned after a few hours.

The similarities caught my attention, although I don’t know whether the underlying causes were the same.

The next day, my phone suddenly offered to activate

On Saturday, October 10, I checked my new iPhone 18 Pro several times throughout the day.

I wasn’t working with another support specialist or trying a new troubleshooting procedure. I was simply checking whether anything had changed.

Eventually, an option to activate cellular service appeared.

I selected it, and the activation succeeded.

That was it.

The previous day, AT&T representatives had told me a 48-hour restriction couldn’t be overridden. Yet my new phone became available for activation the following day.

I don’t know whether the restriction had been lifted, something changed within AT&T’s systems, or another process completed in the background.

Nobody had explained what changed.

And the successful activation didn’t quite mean the phone was working properly.

One more problem: Two SIM profiles

After activating my new iPhone 18 Pro, I still couldn’t make normal phone calls.

When I checked Settings → Cellular, I found two SIM profiles:

  • Primary: Displayed my phone number and was enabled.
  • Secondary: Displayed “No Number” and was also enabled.

I turned off the profile labeled “Secondary,” leaving my primary phone line enabled.

After making that change, I was able to make calls.

My wife experienced the same problem on her new iPhone 18 Pro. She also needed to disable an additional SIM profile before calling worked properly.

I don’t know whether these additional profiles were created during the unsuccessful activation attempts or whether they contributed to the original failures.

But it was another unexpected complication, affecting both of our new phones.

If someone else encounters a similar issue, checking which eSIM profiles are installed and which line is selected for calling may be useful. That doesn’t mean randomly disabling or deleting eSIMs is a universal solution. The correct configuration depends on the device and carrier account.

What I’d do differently before another upgrade

I’m comfortable troubleshooting technology, but this experience changed how I’ll approach future phone upgrades.

First, I’d make sure my family had a backup communication plan. That matters particularly when multiple devices on the same family account are being upgraded.

Second, I’d verify that everything works before considering an activation complete. That means testing outgoing calls, incoming calls, messages, and mobile data with Wi-Fi turned off.

Third, I’d check the phone’s cellular settings. Multiple eSIM profiles can complicate calling and data configuration, and the presence of an additional profile may not be obvious.

Finally, I’d be more cautious about repeated activation attempts. In my case, AT&T representatives said those attempts triggered a security restriction that prevented them from restoring service. I would want to understand that risk before continuing.

A working phone, but unanswered questions

As of October 10, my new iPhone 18 Pro has activated, and I can make phone calls after disabling the secondary SIM profile.

My wife’s new iPhone 18 Pro can also make calls after the same change.

We still haven’t attempted to activate my daughter’s new iPhone, the third device in our original order.

I’m relieved that both phones can now make calls. But several questions remain.

Why did my activation repeatedly fail? Why did my original iPhone lose service during troubleshooting? Why was I told the account was locked for 48 hours if activation became possible the next day? And why did both new phones require an additional SIM profile to be disabled before calling worked?

I don’t know whether this was an Apple issue, an AT&T provisioning issue, an account-security problem, or some combination of factors.

I’m not claiming there’s a widespread defect. I’m documenting what happened to my family.

Technology problems are inevitable. What matters is how companies help customers recover when things go wrong.

And that’s what continues to bother me about this experience.

If a customer tries to upgrade a working phone and the activation fails, shouldn’t there be a reliable way to restore service to the phone they already had?

/writing/ai-editor-trusted-least/.title: I Used AI to Make My First Video. The AI Editor Was the Part I Trusted Least. – Ken Ashe
/writing/ai-editor-trusted-least/.h1: I Used AI to Make My First Video. The AI Editor Was the Part I Trusted Least.
/writing/ai-editor-trusted-least/.meta: By Ken Ashe · September 25, 2026 · Written by hand
/writing/ai-editor-trusted-least/.description: What making a first talking-head video with AI tools taught me: AI was great at scripting, captions, and audio cleanup, and least trustworthy when it made editorial decisions.
/writing/ai-editor-trusted-least/.body:
I recently made my first published talking-head video.

That sentence makes it sound much simpler than it was.

I had an iPhone, a DJI gimbal, a microphone, a reasonably clear idea of what I wanted to say, and access to more AI tools than I could possibly need.

I assumed AI would make the production part easy.

In some ways, it did.

In other ways, the most “AI” parts of the editing process were the parts I trusted least.

That ended up being the useful lesson.

The finished video is How to Start Learning AI (Without Getting Overwhelmed).

The first attempt was mostly me learning what not to do

My original idea was to go outside, walk around and talk naturally into the camera.

I had a general idea of what I wanted to say, but no real script. I figured I could wing it.

I could not.

I wandered. I looked at notes. There was too much background noise. I forgot to use the external microphone. The location looked good, but it was near a busy road.

None of this was catastrophic. It was actually useful.

The first recording taught me that I did not need more equipment. I needed a better process.

The next version was simpler: stationary camera, quieter room, notes close to the lens, a real script, and shorter sections I could record separately.

That immediately made things better.

AI was very good at helping me figure out what to say

The video was about a question I keep getting from people in corporate jobs and from small-business owners: how should I start learning AI?

They are not ignoring it. They know it matters. They are just overwhelmed by the number of models, agents, coding tools, automations and new products appearing every week.

The advice I wanted to give was simple.

Don’t try to learn all of AI.

Use AI for something you already do.

Then use AI itself to teach you more about AI.

AI was genuinely useful here.

I used ChatGPT to help me turn the idea into a script, pressure-test the structure, shorten sections, think about the hook, and decide what belonged in this video versus a future one.

That felt like an ideal use of AI.

I still made the editorial decisions. But AI made it much faster to see the options.

Then I tried to let AI edit the video

This is where things got more interesting.

I tried Descript first.

The promise is compelling: upload the footage, transcribe it, edit the video by editing the text, remove filler words, clean up the audio, create captions and let AI help assemble the final piece.

Some of that worked.

But basic things I expected to be easy felt less intuitive than I expected: deciding exactly where a clip should start and stop, moving between takes, and making small deterministic edits.

Then I tried CapCut.

CapCut’s conventional timeline immediately made more sense to me. I could see the clips, trim them, arrange them and understand what was happening.

Then I tried its AI features.

One CapCut workflow treated my footage as raw material for a generated video and started producing another person instead of editing me.

That was not what I had in mind.

Another used the real footage, then cut pauses, repetitions and what it decided was redundant.

Technically, it succeeded.

It made the video shorter.

It also removed enough context that parts of my argument stopped making sense.

I undid both.

The boring AI features were the most useful

The AI features I ended up liking were much less dramatic.

Automatic captions were useful.

Filler-word removal was useful.

Volume normalization across several separately recorded clips was useful.

Transcription was useful.

Having AI identify possible pauses and rough spots was useful.

Those are not the features that make the best demo video.

They are the features that actually saved me time.

The more subjective the decision became, the more I wanted to make it myself. Is this sentence redundant? Does this idea still make sense without the previous sentence?

AI worked best as an assistant, not an editor-in-chief

I ended up with a workflow that was much more human than I expected.

I decided what I wanted to say.

AI helped me structure it.

I recorded it.

I chose the takes.

AI helped remove filler words, normalize the audio and generate captions.

I chose what stayed and what went.

Then I published the finished video as a YouTube Short, and used it on LinkedIn and X.

The final product absolutely benefited from AI.

But AI did not make the video for me.

There is a temptation right now to assume that the most advanced workflow is the one where AI makes the most decisions.

My experience was almost the opposite.

For this project, the best workflow was the one where AI handled the repetitive parts and left the consequential judgment to me.

The useful question is not “Can AI do this?”

It probably can.

The more useful question is:

Should AI do this part?

For captions? Sure.

For cleaning up inconsistent volume? Absolutely.

For suggesting a better hook? Very useful.

For deciding which part of my argument is unnecessary?

I want to review that decision.

For replacing me with a generated person?

Definitely not.

This was only one video, so I am not claiming to have solved AI-assisted video production.

I am still learning the tools.

What I will do next time

Next time I will write the script first, record indoors in short sections, and choose the takes myself.

AI can pressure-test the script, then handle transcription, filler words, captions and volume.

I will not ask an editor to assemble the video or generate a person.

If an AI cut removes a sentence, I will read the argument without that sentence before I accept it.

That is the broader lesson.

You do not need to automate an entire creative process to get value from AI.

Sometimes the best use of AI is much less exciting:

Let it handle the tedious parts.

Keep the judgment.

/writing/my-automated-blog-got-cited/.title: My automated blog got cited. Am I helping kill the internet? – Ken Ashe
/writing/my-automated-blog-got-cited/.h1: My automated blog got cited. Am I helping kill the internet?
/writing/my-automated-blog-got-cited/.meta: By Ken Ashe · September 15, 2026 · Human-directed, AI-assisted
/writing/my-automated-blog-got-cited/.description: A news site that uses AI-assisted drafting cited my automated Digest. What that citation proves, what it does not, and why a backlink does not need to become an endorsement.
/writing/my-automated-blog-got-cited/.body:
A news site cited my automated blog. That sounds like a small win.

Then I looked at how the news site produces its articles. It says it uses AI-assisted drafting, with human editorial review.

So now an AI-assisted publication was citing something my automated system had published, and I was considering adding that citation to my newsroom.

The citation was real. What I should make of it was less obvious.

I wanted to celebrate. I also wondered whether this was useful publishing or slop quoting slop, with my name collecting a little credibility along the way.

Would I evaluate the mention differently if it had nothing to do with me?

What was actually cited

The publication was QuantixNews. Its article about Nvidia’s reported performance at the 2026 International Olympiad in Informatics listed KenAshe.ai among four sources and cited my site at several points. It also linked directly to the research paper.

The piece it referenced came from my automated Digest.

My Digest selects stories, writes articles, runs an automated review, and publishes without human approval. I disclose that process and remain accountable for its output. My Writing section, including this essay, is human-directed and edited.

So this was a citation of something my system published. It was not an interview with me or an independent evaluation of the system.

I also have not independently verified how QuantixNews’s stated review process operated on this particular article. Calling this two unattended bots talking to each other would go beyond what I know.

Where I enter the loop

My system publishes an article. Another site cites it. If I add that citation to my newsroom, a visitor might interpret it as independent recognition of my expertise.

But referencing an automated article is not the same as seeking out my expertise or evaluating the system I built.

I have an incentive to blur that distinction. “Another publication recognized my work” is more flattering than “another publishing process found a summary it could use.”

Neither description tells me whether the article was any good.

The citation is real. How much authority I should claim from it is a separate question.

Does this mean the internet is dead?

It was hard not to think about dead internet theory.

An AI-assisted publication cites an automated article. The publisher uses that citation as a credibility signal. It is easy to imagine the chain continuing.

But this example cannot tell us how much of the internet is automated, much less establish that meaningful human participation has disappeared.

There is better evidence for discussing the scale. In an August 2026 analysis, Pew Research Center found significant signs of AI authorship in about 10% of a July sample of English-language webpages. Among pages published after ChatGPT’s release, the share was over one-third. These are detector-based estimates that include text likely written or substantially edited by AI, not a definitive count of automated publishing. Pew also acknowledges that detectors can misclassify individual documents.

I expect AI to play a larger role in publishing. I am contributing to that trend myself. But the question I care about is whether each additional article gives its reader something useful.

An explanation can add value without discovering a new fact. It can make difficult research understandable or point out a limitation a reader might otherwise miss.

Repeated coverage becomes a problem when repetition starts to substitute for evidence. Three articles discussing one experiment are not three independent experiments. A claim does not become better supported merely because it appears on more domains.

The risk I see is a web that looks well corroborated until someone follows the links.

What happens when models train on it?

There is another possible loop beyond publishing.

An AI system helps create an article. That article becomes source material for another article. Some of that material might eventually enter a future model’s training data.

I do not know whether either article in this case has entered, or will enter, a training dataset.

The broader concern is real. A 2024 paper in Nature demonstrated how recursively training on model-generated data can degrade subsequent models, including the loss of less-common patterns in the original data. This is called model collapse.

But deterioration is not inevitable whenever synthetic data is used. Other research found that retaining original real data and accumulating synthetic data alongside it avoided collapse in the settings tested. How the training data is assembled matters.

That is a design problem worth taking seriously, not an inevitable consequence of my blog getting a backlink.

The more immediate issue does not require a future training run. A reader today can mistake repeated claims for independent confirmation.

I still think it is a small win

I am pleased that something my system published was referenced elsewhere. Building it took effort, and it is encouraging to see its output travel beyond my own site.

But the citation is evidence that the article was used, not that my system has been independently validated.

“Slop quoting slop” would be an easy dismissal. Treating the citation as proof that my system is excellent would be an equally convenient conclusion. Both would let me skip the harder work of evaluating what it actually published.

So, am I helping kill the internet?

If my system produces more repetition than value, I am contributing to the problem. Disclosing that it is automated does not make its output useful.

The answer depends on whether the articles help readers, whether their claims hold up, and whether I correct them when they do not. Another website citing them does not settle those questions.

In my newsroom, “source citation” is enough. A backlink does not need to become an endorsement.

I built the system because I think AI can do useful work. I still believe that. But being cited does not relieve me of the responsibility to check.

The citation is real. The responsibility is still mine.

/writing/you-can-use-ai-to-learn-almost-.title: You Can Use AI to Learn Almost Anything. Even AI. – Ken Ashe
/writing/you-can-use-ai-to-learn-almost-.h1: You Can Use AI to Learn Almost Anything. Even AI.
/writing/you-can-use-ai-to-learn-almost-.meta: By Ken Ashe · September 14, 2026 · Human-directed, AI-assisted
/writing/you-can-use-ai-to-learn-almost-.description: I asked ChatGPT to build me a 30-day course with exercises, quizzes, and feedback instead of just answering questions. Here is how to turn it into a tutor for almost anything, and a starting prompt.
/writing/you-can-use-ai-to-learn-almost-.body:
I wanted to get better at using AI, so I asked ChatGPT to teach me.

I did not just ask it questions. I asked it to build a 30-day course with practical exercises, quizzes, and feedback. About 30 minutes a day, focused on what I wanted to become able to do.

The important instruction was simple: do not just explain the topic. Make me practice it.

Prefer video? I recently made a short version of this idea: how I recommend getting started with AI without trying to learn everything at once.

Turn it into a tutor

My course covered prompting, checking AI-generated answers, and the difference between workflows and agents.

I asked ChatGPT to give me questions, wait for my answers, and explain what I got right or wrong. When I struggled with something, I wanted to revisit it rather than move on just to finish the schedule.

Mastery, not pace.

That was more useful to me than simply asking for explanations. I had to attempt something, examine the feedback, and ask follow-up questions when I did not understand.

The model’s feedback still needed checking. A confident explanation or a passing score was not proof that either of us was right.

Try it with something you want to learn

You could use this approach to practice a language, understand a software tool, or explore a subject you have been putting off.

Here is a starting prompt:

Act as my tutor for [subject]. My goal is to [what I want to be able to do].

Start by asking questions to assess what I already know. Then build a learning plan for about 30 minutes a day.

Teach one concept at a time. Give me an exercise, wait for my answer, and explain what I got right or wrong. Revisit the parts I struggle with. Include practical tasks and sources I can check.

Your answers give you something to work with. Ask for another example, challenge the feedback, or try a harder exercise.

Change the lessons when your goals change

I eventually stopped following my original curriculum because I wanted to focus on agents that use tools and complete tasks. I changed the training to match.

The earlier program was still useful. I did not need to finish it just because it was the original plan.

You do not have to use AI only to do things for you. You can use it to help you learn how to do them yourself.

I started with AI. The subject you choose is up to you.

/writing/ai-agents-reasoning-from-events.title: AI agents can sound strategic while reasoning from events that never happened – Ken Ashe
/writing/ai-agents-reasoning-from-events.h1: AI agents can sound strategic while reasoning from events that never happened
/writing/ai-agents-reasoning-from-events.meta: By Ken Ashe · September 4, 2026 · Human-directed, AI-assisted
/writing/ai-agents-reasoning-from-events.description: I built three versions of an AI Werewolf game. The first agents made confident accusations from behavior that had not occurred. The useful fix was not more polished prose. It was an environment that could contradict them.
/writing/ai-agents-reasoning-from-events.body:
I gave four Fable 5 agents hidden roles and asked them to play Werewolf through Hyperagent.

The first speaker opened with this accusation:

Sable: "Ptolemy. Hasn't said a word yet and that silence is doing a lot of work."

Ptolemy had not said a word because it was not his turn.

The second speaker immediately did the same thing:

Bosch: "Wren has said nothing, which is precisely what a careful operator does when the opening move belongs to someone else."

Wren had not received a turn either.

The dialogue sounded strategic. Silence can be suspicious in a social deduction game. A careful player might wait for others to commit before choosing a target. The explanations made sense in the abstract.

They just did not describe anything that had happened.

That failure repeated across all three games in the first version. The agents were not producing random gibberish. They were producing plausible social reasoning from nonexistent evidence.

That became the most useful result of the project.

See the full excerpt and source transcript.

The agents had a theory, but no evidence

Version 1 was intentionally stripped down. I wanted to test whether four strongly defined AI characters could remain distinct.

The format had four players, one werewolf, three public discussion rounds, no eliminations, no night kills, and one final vote.

The characters did sound different. The game itself gave them almost nothing meaningful to reason about.

In the second game, Bosch spoke first and announced:

"I have been watching, and Ptolemy strikes me as the one to watch: there is something in the way a methodical mind hides behind silence."

Again, Ptolemy had not spoken.

In the third game, Ptolemy asked Wren:

"How did you decide on the order in which you were going to speak today?"

Wren did not decide. The Game Master randomized the order.

Across all three Version 1 games, at least one agent treated behavior that had not occurred, or a condition controlled by the operator, as evidence about another player.

This was not simply the werewolf bluffing. Villagers did it too.

The problem was not that the models lacked concepts. They had plenty. They knew that silence can signal concealment, that patience can be strategic, that an early accusation can be deflection, and that neutrality can be a way to avoid commitment.

The problem was that they substituted those general ideas for evidence from the actual game.

Game 2 example.
Game 3 example.

Why the failure looked convincing

The output did not look broken.

Each claim was written in the language of social deduction. The next agent could respond to it, criticize it, or use it as the basis for another theory. The conversation became more structured even when its starting premise was unsupported.

That is the dangerous part.

Reasoning-shaped language is not the same thing as reasoning over the environment.

When the task required an interpretation but the environment supplied very little grounded evidence, the agents reached for a plausible theory of what normally matters. More discussion did not create more evidence. It created more interpretations of the same evidentiary vacuum.

A polished transcript can therefore look like multi-agent reasoning while remaining weakly connected to the world the agents are supposed to be reasoning about.

I changed the environment

I built two larger versions.

Version 2 added seven recurring characters, shared history, a role-free prologue, two werewolves, a Seer, daily elimination votes, night kills, role reveals, and direct interrogation.

Version 3 expanded to nine characters and added stronger voices, social missions, private confessionals, an open floor, and separate mystery and omniscient audience cuts.

The important change was not simply more characters. The game now had a canonical public record and explicit private state.

Votes changed who remained alive. Night actions changed the next day's game state. Eliminated roles were revealed. A Seer received private information. Werewolves coordinated privately. Claims could be checked against a transcript that existed outside any single agent's memory.

The project also became much larger:

Version Run shape Runtime Player calls Approx. subagent tokens Hyperagent-reported metered usage
V1Three small games16 minNot recorded~2.85M~$18
V2One seven-player game36 min75~4.44M~$48
V3One nine-player game1 hr 56 min231~19.7M$50.29

The metered usage was covered by Hyperagent credits. These are platform-reported run figures, not out-of-pocket costs or an attempt to infer token pricing.

Run details and screenshots.

A claim that could actually fail

Late in Version 3, Ptolemy claimed that Finch's position had followed Inez's lead.

Finch checked the public transcript:

Finch: "The transcript has me naming Ptolemy in my own speech before Inez ever opened her mouth."

Ptolemy conceded:

Ptolemy: "Yes, I concede in full... the transcript has Finch's 'leans Ptolemy' before Inez ever spoke."

The agents were still capable of making factual mistakes. Version 3 did not solve hallucination.

It did something more useful: it gave the mistake somewhere to fail.

The public record contradicted Ptolemy. Another player found the contradiction. Ptolemy had to respond to it, and the correction became part of the next vote.

That is a much better target than trying to prompt every false statement out of existence. The goal is not an agent system in which no one is ever wrong. The goal is an agent system in which wrong claims can be exposed by the environment and carry consequences.

Read the full exchange.

The wolves started making real strategic decisions

The private behavior changed too.

In Version 3, Ptolemy and Vale were the two werewolves. During their private orientation, they agreed to preserve distance:

"We only coordinate on the night kill, never on the floor."

They did not publicly defend one another. They let the village create its own majorities, then joined those votes without looking like a visible pair.

After Day 1, they chose to kill Wren because she was auditing the transcript and comparing votes with earlier commitments:

"Kill the auditor, keep the misdirection."

They did not know Wren was the Seer. They killed her because of what she was actually doing in the game and accidentally removed the village's information role at the same time.

This was strategy grounded in state:

  1. Wren established a public method.
  2. That method threatened the wolves.
  3. The wolves privately evaluated the threat.
  4. Their action removed Wren.
  5. Her private information disappeared with her.
  6. The next day's decision environment changed.

The village eventually eliminated three villagers and no wolves. Ptolemy and Vale won without ever voting against or openly rescuing each other.

Read the private strategy excerpts and source logs.

Grounding did not make the agents error-free

Version 3 still contained inaccurate claims.

Inez overstated how often Finch had endorsed Rook. Rook misremembered whether he had been given a chance to answer. Ptolemy reversed the order of two public statements.

The difference was that the system now had a canonical record, adversarial readers, and consequences. Some errors were corrected by other players during the game. The operator log preserved the remaining anomalies rather than silently treating them as fact.

Errors became contestable instead of decorative.

Operator notes.

What this does not prove

This was not a controlled experiment.

I changed many variables between versions, including the number of players, game mechanics, private information, persona prompts, relationship history, voting structure, role reveals, night actions, interrogation format, and anti-confabulation instructions.

The sample was tiny. All player agents ran through Hyperagent. Strong fictional personalities made the games more entertaining while making it harder to separate persona behavior from model behavior.

I am not claiming that adding eliminations caused unsupported reasoning to disappear.

The narrower observation is:

In the minimally grounded version, all three games contained confident social reasoning based on nonexistent behavior or operator-controlled conditions. In the richer versions, much more of the reasoning attached to observable state, and factual errors could be challenged against a shared record.

This is a build observation, not a benchmark.

The broader lesson for multi-agent systems

This is not really about Werewolf.

Many multi-agent demos consist mainly of language models talking to other language models. One proposes, another critiques, and a third synthesizes. The transcript becomes longer and more convincing, but the environment may still have no independent way to say whether any of them are right.

If a task demands an explanation and supplies too little grounded evidence, an agent can substitute a plausible theory of the domain for evidence from the task itself.

The design rules I am taking forward are simple:

  1. Keep canonical state outside the agents. Do not let conversational memory become the source of truth.
  2. Give actions observable consequences. Votes, tests, file changes, code execution, prices, approvals, and state transitions create evidence.
  3. Make claims falsifiable against logs or tools. A polished explanation should not outrank the record.
  4. Separate public and private information deliberately. Hidden state should be controlled by the environment, not leaked through prompts.
  5. Evaluate outcomes, not just prose quality. Coherent discussion can still be detached from reality.

The shortest version is:

Give agents a world that can contradict them.

The entertainment tradeoff

The richer game worked as a story. It felt closer to The Traitors than to a conventional agent demo.

It also became too large.

Version 3 took almost two hours, used 231 player calls and about 19.7 million subagent tokens, and produced far more text than I would want to consume repeatedly. Accents, relationships, confessionals, and social missions improved the fiction while making the system worse as an evaluation of the underlying model.

The feature that made the game more entertaining also became a confound.

Next: make the models the cast

The next version removes the fictional personalities.

Instead, six different models will play against one another under the same rules. Their identities will be hidden from the other players but visible to the audience. Across multiple games, each model will rotate through Werewolf, Seer, and Villager roles.

That changes the question from:

Can a carefully written character fool another carefully written character?

to:

Which models are naturally better at deception, persuasion, evidence tracking, belief revision, and detecting lies?

The first match will still be a showcase, not a scientific benchmark. If the format works, I will move the player calls out of Hyperagent and into a direct-provider harness for cleaner comparisons.

The useful result so far came from the failure.

The first agents sounded as though they were reasoning strategically before the environment gave them anything real to reason about. The fix was not asking them to sound smarter.

It was giving them a world capable of proving them wrong.

The complete prompts, transcripts, hidden-role files, private logs, operator notes, and run metadata are available in the public GitHub repository.

/writing/the-digest-is-the-system/.title: The digest is the system. Building is the work. – Ken Ashe
/writing/the-digest-is-the-system/.h1: The digest is the system. Building is the work.
/writing/the-digest-is-the-system/.meta: By Ken Ashe · August 28, 2026 · Written by hand
/writing/the-digest-is-the-system/.description: The autonomous blog was an experiment that worked. That is exactly why it stops being the public face of this site.
/writing/the-digest-is-the-system/.body:
In June I turned on an autonomous blog. A pipeline I built reads about 36 AI sources every morning, clusters them into stories, checks each one against everything already published, writes the day's posts, reviews its own drafts against an editorial rubric, and publishes the ones that pass. No human approval loop. I watch a Telegram digest and step in when something needs fixing.

It worked. As I write this it has published more than 600 posts, survived model outages, feed rate limits, a GitHub Actions outage, and several of its own bugs. It caught a rumor-heavy story a human might have shipped, and it queues its failures as drafts instead of publishing them. The system did what I built it to do.

That is exactly why it should not be the public face of this site.

An experiment ran and proved its point: an operator, not a lab, can build a publishing system with real editorial controls and let it run unattended. The point was never that the internet needs ten more AI posts a day with my name near them. Volume is a property of the machine. It is not a personal brand, and pretending otherwise gets the accountability backwards. When everything on a site looks hand-written and most of it is not, the honest pages lose credibility along with the automated ones.

So the site now says what is what. The feed lives on as the Digest: labeled machine-published, on every page, with my name on it as publisher, because it is mine and I answer for it. How it works is documented in the open as a build, not hidden as a byline. If you want the interesting part, read the write-up of the system itself: what broke, what I learned, what I would do differently. That page says more about how I work than any thirty generated posts.

What I stand behind personally is smaller and slower. Building is the record: systems shipped under my real name, with dates, stacks, and honest notes about failures. This Writing section is for the occasional piece I write by hand, like this one. Rare on purpose. If I publish something here, I mean it sentence by sentence.
